Hollingsworth v. Perry. In June 2013, the Supreme Court ruled five to four to invalidate California's Proposition 8 on standing grounds, effectively voiding the state's same-sex marriage ban without establishing a nationwide constitutional right to marriage. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, which focused on a procedural question rather than the merits of marriage equality. Roberts held that the official proponents of Proposition 8 lacked constitutional standing to defend the measure in federal court when California's governor and attorney general declined to appeal the lower court ruling that had struck it down. He emphasized that the Court had never before upheld the standing of a private party to defend the constitutionality of a state statute when state officials chose not to. Because the decision turned entirely on standing rather than the constitutional merits, it did not establish a right to same-sex marriage nationwide. Justice Kennedy wrote a concurrence that outlined the constitutional case for marriage equality, presaging what his majority opinion would accomplish in Obergefell just two years later. The dissenters argued that the proponents of Proposition 8 had cognizable standing as the architects and defenders of the measure. Though limited in scope, Hollingsworth cleared the way for Obergefell to complete the work of establishing marriage equality across all fifty states.
